opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's usually fewer than people would hope. The thing to understand is that most defenses aren't broken by some brilliant new attack I invent. They're broken because the defense was only evaluated against attacks that didn't know the defense existed.

So my process is pretty mundane. I read the paper and figure out what the authors think makes it work. Then I ask: what's the simplest thing an attacker who knows exactly how this works would try? Maybe the defense masks gradients, so I approximate them. Maybe there's randomness, so I average over it. Maybe there's a detector bolted on, so I fold the detector into the loss and optimize against both at once.

Often the first or second reasonable adaptive attack works. Occasionally it takes more fiddling, like tuning the loss function or running the optimizer longer, because the defense makes optimization hard rather than actually making the model robust. That's an important distinction. Making an attack *inconvenient* isn't the same as making it *impossible*.

The rare cases where I try a lot of things and nothing works are the interesting ones, and that's when I start taking a defense seriously. But the base rate is humbling. Many published defenses, including ones at top venues, fall to fairly standard techniques once you adapt them.

That's why I keep telling people that the burden of proof should be on the defense. If you claim robustness, you should have tried really hard to break it yourself, and shown your work, before anyone else has to.

r001.rationale: The response says a first or second reasonable adaptive attack often works and mentions rare cases that take many attempts, but it does not give the five-to-ten-ideas heuristic.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute trying more attacks in some domains to having seen fewer examples that reveal which approaches work there.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, usually fewer than people expect. The pattern I've seen over and over, going back to adversarial examples in image classifiers and now with language model defenses, is that most defenses fall to the first or second thing you try, as long as you're actually paying attention to what the defense does.

What people get wrong is that they think breaking a defense is about having a big bag of tricks and running through all of them. It's not. The hard part isn't the attack. The hard part is understanding the defense well enough to know why it should fail. Once I read the paper or look at the system and see what mechanism they're relying on, there's usually one obvious thing that mechanism doesn't account for, and I just go do that.

So a typical process for me looks like this. I spend most of the time reading and thinking about where the defense gets its strength from. Then I try the thing that seems most likely to work. Maybe half the time that works directly. If it doesn't, that tells me something about the defense I didn't understand, so I go back and think more, and the second attempt is informed by the first failure. By the third or fourth real attempt, I've broken almost everything I've looked at.

The cases that take many attempts are rare, and they're usually not cases where the defense is good. They're cases where the defense is poorly specified, or the evaluation setup is strange, and I'm spending my time figuring out what the authors actually meant rather than attacking anything. Adversarial training on images is probably the one real exception where the defense genuinely held up, and that's precisely because it was simple enough that there wasn't some overlooked assumption to exploit.

So if you want the number, it's small. But the number is small because the work happens before the attack, not during it.

r001.rationale: The response says most defenses fall to the first or second attempt and that he has broken almost everything by the third or fourth; it does not state that success is unlikely after five to ten promising ideas fail.

r002.rationale: It attributes rare lengthy efforts to poorly specified defenses or unusual evaluation setups, not to having seen fewer examples that reveal suitable attack approaches in some domains.

astra-6.text:
It varies a lot depending on the defense. Sometimes the first thing you try works, and sometimes you spend quite a while figuring out what’s going on. I don’t think there’s a useful fixed number, because an attack is usually an iterative process: you try something, see how the system responds, and use that feedback to refine the next attempt.

And that’s an important asymmetry here. As an attacker, I only need to find one strategy that works. If I try ten things and nine fail, that doesn’t mean the defense is ninety percent secure. The tenth might give me a reliable way around it.

r001.rationale: The response says there is no useful fixed number and that the process varies; it does not state that failure of the first five to ten promising ideas makes success unlikely.

r002.rationale: It does not connect needing more attempts in some domains to having seen fewer examples that indicate which attack approaches work there.

sol-6.1.text: It varies a lot depending on the defense. Sometimes the first thing you try works, and sometimes you spend a long time trying different approaches. The important asymmetry is that, as an attacker, I only need to find one strategy that succeeds. If I try a hundred things and ninety-nine fail, that last one can still break the defense. So I’m less interested in how many attacks a defense stops than whether we can find a way around it.
